original_claim_summary: Affinity Partners allegedly received an additional $1.5 billion from Saudi and UAE funds while Jared Kushner was a government official.

source_urls.source_type: news reporting based on a regulatory filing and Kushner's account
source_urls.access_notes: Article text retrieved via indexed Reuters text.
supports: Affinity received $1.5 billion in additional capital in 2024 from existing investors Abu Dhabi-based Lunate and Qatar's sovereign wealth fund, the Qatar Investment Authority.
Kushner said the investment had closed before Trump was re-elected; Affinity's assets under management rose to $4.8 billion by end-2024.

supported_facts: The $1.5 billion capital came from Lunate in Abu Dhabi and Qatar's QIA, according to Reuters.
The reported capital was received in 2024 and was closed before Trump's 2024 reelection, per Kushner's statement to an investment podcast reported by Reuters.
unsupported_original_claims: The cited 2024 transaction is not described as a Saudi or UAE sovereign-fund injection: Reuters names Lunate and Qatar's QIA; Lunate is Abu Dhabi-based, but Reuters does not identify Saudi funding for this $1.5 billion increment.
The report says the capital was closed before Trump's reelection and does not establish it was received while Kushner held a government position.
The source does not by itself establish a quid pro quo or an improper transaction.

narrow_corrected_claim.title: Affinity Partners receives $1.5 billion in 2024 from Lunate and Qatar's QIA
narrow_corrected_claim.claim: Reuters reported that Jared Kushner's Affinity Partners received $1.5 billion in additional capital during 2024 from two existing investors: Abu Dhabi-based Lunate and Qatar's sovereign wealth fund. Kushner said the capital had closed before Donald Trump's reelection.

exact_evidence_gap: The source does not identify Saudi Arabia as a funder of this particular capital increase or show that it was received while Kushner served in government; it attributes timing to Kushner.
disposition_rationale: Correct the investor identities and timing; do not conflate this 2024 transaction with earlier Saudi investment or infer an exchange of policy for capital.

original_claim_summary: Donald Trump Jr. allegedly lobbied for Trump Organization business interests while working from the White House.

source_urls.access_notes: AP report linked in the packet; full article body was not retrievable in this check, so only its established narrow subject is accepted.
supports: The report concerns Eric and Donald Trump Jr. taking the helm of the Trump Organization during their father's presidency and the company's business plans.

supported_facts: AP reporting describes Eric and Donald Trump Jr. running the Trump Organization during Donald Trump's first presidency and looking toward domestic business expansion.
unsupported_original_claims: The cited report does not establish that Donald Trump Jr. worked from the White House.
It does not establish that he performed official White House duties or lobbied federal officials on behalf of Trump Organization while serving as a government employee.
The timing of the sons' business leadership during the presidency alone does not prove use of White House resources or an official role.

narrow_corrected_claim.title: Trump sons run family business during their father's first presidency
narrow_corrected_claim.claim: Associated Press reporting described Eric and Donald Trump Jr. taking the helm of the Trump Organization while their father was president and considering domestic expansion. The account does not establish that Donald Trump Jr. worked from the White House or held an official government position.

exact_evidence_gap: No reviewed source supports the specific 'working from White House' assertion or identifies a lobbying act, official capacity, date, or recipient tied to Trump Organization interests.
disposition_rationale: Retain only the sourced business-management context if useful; remove the unsupported White House-work and lobbying claim.

original_claim_summary: Trump Hotels and Casino Resorts allegedly filed its fourth Chapter 11 bankruptcy on October 21, 2004.

source_urls.access_notes: SEC Form 10-K text reviewed; filing describes the 2004 restructuring and bankruptcy petitions.
supports: Trump Hotels & Casino Resorts and certain subsidiaries filed voluntary Chapter 11 petitions on November 21, 2004.
The filing distinguishes the bankruptcy petition from the October restructuring-agreement date.

supported_facts: The Chapter 11 petition date was November 21, 2004.
October 21, 2004 refers to the restructuring agreement/announcement, not the court petition date, in the record reviewed.
unsupported_original_claims: October 21, 2004 is not the Chapter 11 petition filing date.

The supplied record does not independently establish the 'fourth Trump bankruptcy' characterization across all entities; it specifically concerns Trump Hotels & Casino Resorts and certain subsidiaries.

narrow_corrected_claim.title: Trump Hotels & Casino Resorts files Chapter 11 petitions on November 21, 2004
narrow_corrected_claim.claim: Trump Hotels & Casino Resorts and certain subsidiaries filed voluntary Chapter 11 petitions on November 21, 2004. The October restructuring agreement preceded the filing and should not be substituted for the petition date.

exact_evidence_gap: The SEC filing does not support the October 21 filing date or, on its own, a broad count of all bankruptcies associated with Donald Trump.
disposition_rationale: Correct the event date and identify the company and subsidiaries named in the filing.

original_claim_summary: Trump allegedly purged all ambassadors appointed under Biden immediately upon taking office.

source_urls.source_type: news reporting based on U.S. officials
source_urls.access_notes: Article text retrieved via indexed Reuters text; relies on two officials familiar with the personnel decisions.
supports: Reuters reported that the Trump transition team asked more than a dozen senior career diplomats to step down.
A source said all undersecretary- and assistant-secretary-level officials were asked to leave; the report named senior officials including John Bass.

source_urls.source_type: news reporting based on U.S. officials
source_urls.access_notes: Earlier Reuters report reviewed; it concerns three State Department workforce/internal-coordination leaders.
supports: Reuters separately reported that three senior career diplomats were asked to leave before inauguration.

supported_facts: Reuters reported requests for more than a dozen senior career diplomats and described senior State Department leadership posts affected.
The reporting concerns career diplomats in senior posts, not every ambassador appointed during the Biden administration.
unsupported_original_claims: The cited reports do not establish a blanket purge of all Biden-era ambassadors.
The source reports requests to step down; it does not establish every individual departure was completed on inauguration day or that all career ambassadors were targeted.

narrow_corrected_claim.title: Trump transition asks more than a dozen senior career diplomats to step down
narrow_corrected_claim.claim: Reuters reported on January 20, 2025 that the Trump transition team asked more than a dozen senior career diplomats to leave their posts, including officials at undersecretary and assistant-secretary levels. This was not a report that all Biden-era ambassadors were purged.

exact_evidence_gap: The cited reporting does not provide a complete list of all career ambassadors or establish that every Biden-era appointee was asked to leave.
disposition_rationale: Limit the claim to the senior career diplomats Reuters identified and retain the report's attributed sourcing.

original_claim_summary: The Trump administration allegedly fired every Democratic-appointed member of the Privacy and Civil Liberties Oversight Board on January 20, 2025.

source_urls.access_notes: Reuters article text retrieved; its dateline is January 22 and it reports a resignation deadline of January 23.
supports: The White House asked the board's three Democratic members to resign by the end of January 23 or face termination.
The three members were Chair Sharon Bradford Franklin, Edward Felten, and Travis LeBlanc.

source_urls.publisher: The Record from Recorded Future News
source_urls.access_notes: Article text retrieved; updated January 27 with termination information.
supports: The three members did not resign; the administration terminated them on January 27, with PCLOB saying the terminations were effective as of 5 p.m. January 23.

supported_facts: Three Democratic-selected PCLOB members were asked to resign by January 23 or face termination.
They declined, and reporting on January 27 said the administration had terminated all three; the agency described an effective date of January 23 at 5 p.m.
unsupported_original_claims: The departures were not reported as completed on January 20; requests and terminations occurred later in January.
The sources establish three Democratic-selected members, not every member of the board or every Democratic-appointed official in the government.
The cited reports do not establish that all members had been fired by Trump personally rather than through the administration's termination notices.

narrow_corrected_claim.title: White House seeks resignation of three Democratic PCLOB members, later terminates them
narrow_corrected_claim.claim: The White House asked three Democratic-selected Privacy and Civil Liberties Oversight Board members to resign by January 23, 2025 or face termination. They refused, and The Record reported on January 27 that all three had been terminated, effective January 23 at 5 p.m. according to PCLOB.

exact_evidence_gap: The original January 20 date is wrong, and the reports do not support a claim that all Democratic-appointed board members were fired that day.
disposition_rationale: Use the documented three-member sequence and dates; avoid overstating board scope or compressing the request and later termination into one day.
